text_content: look davao's la verna flood control basin site c to hold almost 11 olympic pools of rainwater construction is moving forward at site c of the three retarding basins rising along la verna creek in buhangin part of the php 211 million flood control project of the department of public works and highways dpwh davao city 3rd district engineering office aerial footage taken on october 9 2026 shows excavators shaping the basin floor beside the existing la verna pumping station along the davao city diversion road cp garcia highway with boulders and steel sheet piles staged on site for the next phase of works once completed site c is designed to hold up to 27,260 cubic meters of stormwater or about 962,679 cubic feet that is almost 11 olympic-size swimming pools worth of capacity from this site alone when all three sites are completed sites a b and c will store a combined 79,460 cubic meters roughly equivalent to 32 olympic-size swimming pools the basins will work hand in hand with the pumping station built in 2019 temporarily holding runoff during heavy rains and releasing it gradually toward the caap outfall the goal is to end the street flooding that has long disrupted traffic in the la verna area keeping one of davao's busiest corridors safe and passable for thousands of daily commuters metro davao rising crown jewel of mindanao davao city danny betonio raneses

champi entered the philippine area of responsibility par at around 10:40 a m tuesday areas under signal no 1 are batanes eastern portion of babuyan islands babuyan is camiguin is didicas is eastern portion of mainland cagayan santa ana gonzaga lal-lo santa teresita camalaniugan aparri buguey gattaran baggao peñablanca northeastern portion of isabela maconacon divilacan palanan san pablo cabagan santa maria tumauini ilagan city and northeastern portion of catanduanes pandan bagamanoc panganiban viga gigmoto it doesn't mean that these areas will immediately feel the effects of the wind signal there are at least 36 hours for the people in these areas to prepare for the strong winds philippine atmospheric geophysical and astronomical services administration pagasa forecaster chris perez said in a press conference the cyclone was located 1,385 kilometers east of central luzon outside of par as of 10 a m it is moving west northwestward at 25 kilometers per hour kph rosal packs maximum sustained winds of 185 kph near the center and gustiness of up to 230 kph it is not directly affecting any part of the country the cyclone is forecast to move towards extreme northern luzon taiwan area in the coming days perez said he said no significant rainfall is expected in the next 24 hours perez however said that in the coming days the wind signal may be raised to no 2 or 3 as rosal moves closer to northern luzon as of tuesday pagasa said the northeasterly windflow and rosal's periphery will cause strong to gale-force gusts across batanes ilocos norte cagayan isabela polillo islands camarines norte camarines sur catanduanes northern samar eastern samar most of caraga camiguin misamis oriental sarangani davao del sur and davao occidental meanwhile the cyclone is forecast to weaken into a typhoon on thursday it is expected to exit par on saturday perez added disaster response meanwhile the office of civil defense ocd called on all authorities and the public to take the necessary measures to limit the impact of rosal in an advisory late monday the ocd urged regional and local disaster risk reduction and management councils to strengthen monitoring review contingency plans preposition response resources and ensure the readiness of personnel equipment evacuation centers and critical facilities it also urged closer monitoring of rainfall river and reservoir levels tides low-lying and landslide-prone areas coordinate early warnings and possible preemptive evacuations and prioritize vulnerable groups including persons with disabilities senior citizens and children the public is advised to monitor official weather bulletins and local government advisories prepare emergency supplies secure essential documents and be ready to evacuate when instructed communities are reminded that the ongoing el niño conditions do not eliminate the risks of sudden heavy rainfall flash floods landslides and other hazards it said thus the need for timely coordinated action and sustained public vigilance to protect lives and minimize the potential impacts of the weather disturbance the philippine national police has also alerted its field units and ordered the activation of disaster response measures in areas affected by rosal with a reports from priam nepomuceno and lloyd caliwan/pna graphics from pagasa

text_content: davao's flood map explained why different neighborhoods face different flood risks when heavy rains hit davao city why do some neighborhoods experience sudden flash floods that recede in a few hours while others remain submerged under standing water for days it all comes down to catchment hydrology the master plan developed by the department of public works and highways dpwh and the japan international cooperation agency jica covers 2,200 square kilometers divided into three main river basins because each catchment has a unique shape slope and size each one poses a completely different flood threat to specific davao neighborhoods 1 davao river basin 1,755 km2 massive volume and standing water neighborhoods affected waan tigatto ma-a barangay 19 barangay 8 and bucana what happens here this is the largest river system in the area because its catchment extends deep into the northern mountain ranges it collects enormous volumes of rainwater even when it isn't raining in the downtown area heavy rainfall up in the mountains eventually travels downstream into the city the engineering reality because the basin is so large there is a time delay before the main wave of water reaches the city as the river passes through tight natural bends near tigatto and ma-a the channel gets squeezed forcing water over the banks worse when peak river flows meet high tides at the river mouth in bucana the seawater acts like a natural dam this creates a severe backwater effect that traps floodwaters inland causing deep slow-draining pools that cover over 480 hectares and affect 43,000 residents 2 matina river basin 70 km2 rapid flash floods and highway bottlenecks neighborhoods affected matina pangi gravahan gsis subdivision and matina crossing what happens here unlike the davao river matina suffers from sudden high-speed flash floods with very little warning time the engineering reality this basin is relatively small steep and heavily built-up with concrete and asphalt because rainwater cannot soak into the ground it immediately rushes straight into the river channel narrow bridge openings-such as the crossing along mcarthur highway-act like narrow bottlenecks when high-volume runoff reaches these tight spots the water backs up rapidly and spills sideways over the banks directly into nearby residential subdivisions 3 talomo river basin 204 km2 raging currents and riverbank collapse neighborhoods affected talomo proper tugbok and communities along the talomo riverbanks what happens here while talomo does not usually create broad standing lakes like the davao river its waters move at extremely high speeds as they surge down from the slopes of mount apo the engineering reality the steep drop in elevation gives the rushing water tremendous kinetic energy instead of long-term standing pools the main danger here is high-velocity water scraping against the riverbed and riverbanks this severe erosion tears away the surrounding land threatens bridge piers and causes steep riverbanks to collapse along the talomo-tugbok corridor 4 the missing gaps intermediate basins and urban creeks neighborhoods affected toril lipadas river bunawan and lasang bunawan/licanan rivers and agdao bajada and buhangin urban creek networks the planning limitation on master plan maps you might notice uncolored spaces between the three big basins in nature land is continuous-every square meter belongs to a catchment the jica study intentionally focused its scope on the three largest high-volume river mains omitting these smaller intermediate catchments why they still matter these smaller watersheds carry severe flood risk for instance the lipadas river in toril causes rapid flash evacuations the bunawan river frequently submerges portions of the davao-agusan highway and dense urban creek networks in agdao and buhangin overflow quickly during short thunderstorms because over 95 percent of the city's natural urban wetlands have been paved over comprehensive city drainage requires addressing these omitted gaps alongside the main rivers the takeaway whether it's standing water along the davao river flash flooding in matina riverbank erosion in talomo or creek overflow in agdao and toril any effective flood strategy must treat all catchments as interconnected systems davao flood control series 4 part deep dive read the full overview post here part 1 davao flood map explained you are here next up part 2 hard engineering interventions retarding ponds river dredging floodwalls and cut-off channels davao city flood control davao hydrology civil engineering urban planning dpwh jica davao city updates

text_content: the hostage blueprint jica masterplan for davao city what if i told you that a blueprint to stop the flooding in davao city is already finished it was designed by some of the best engineers in the world printed and is currently sitting on a desk in manila here is the truth about the jica master plan the political war currently holding it hostage and what our local government unit lgu is doing to keep our heads above water while we wait the real solution the jica master plan back in 2018 the philippine government partnered with the japan international cooperation agency jica to solve our city's flooding instead of just building basic concrete walls which easily overflow the japanese and local engineers designed a massive city-wide system the core of the plan involves digging massive retarding basins giant empty catch-ponds built in the uplands when a storm hits millions of gallons of water would flow into these basins and be held there safely trapping the water before it ever reaches barangays like ma-a matina and talomo it is brilliant it is proven and it is ready but just look at the timeline of how it got stuck in politics here is the timeline april 2019 the study begins the philippine government and the japan international cooperation agency jica sign an agreement to create a long-term multi-basin master plan 2018-2022 why wasn't it built under duterte a common question is why this wasn't funded during former president rodrigo duterte's term the answer is engineering reality the japanese engineers were still studying our rivers you cannot fund or construct a mega-project when the architects haven't finished the blueprints july 2023 the blueprint is finished jica officially completes the master plan instead of basic walls it proposes php 41.7 billion to build massive retarding basins giant empty bowls upstream to catch and hold storm water before it hits our urban barangays august 9 2024 vp sara calls out the missing budget vice president sara duterte issues a strong public statement pointing out the lack of government action she calls out the current administration for refusing to fund the finalized master plan questioning if the budget is being intentionally withheld simply because the sitting mayor is a duterte baka naman may alinlangan pa hinggil dito dahil duterte ang mayor at mas mamarapatin nilang gibain na lang she stated 2025 present still waiting for funds despite the blueprint being ready for over two years the national government has still not released the funding needed to actually build it bureaucracy or sabotage while politicians debate whether the delay is just standard government red tape for a foreign loan or a deliberate political attack to damage the duterte family ordinary davaoeños are the collateral damage we are the ones sweeping mud out of our homes the ultimate solution to our flooding is being treated as a political football what is the lgu doing while we wait the davao city local government cannot afford a php 41.7 billion mega-project on its own they cannot single-handedly buy multi-hectare lands to build giant retarding ponds without national funding however they are not just sitting around waiting for our government without the big blueprint the lgu is focusing heavily on immediate urban drainage nature-based mitigation and survival here is what the city is doing right now aggressive drainage and inlet upgrades the city engineer's office ceo and task force drainage are continuously ripping up flood-prone choke points in 2025 alone they funded five new major inlet projects to help water subside faster on critical roads like diversion road fronting panacan cemetery quezon boulevard and cabantian-bunawan preventing blockages the city's ancillary services unit asu is conducting aggressive year-round desilting and garbage clearing of these new drainage systems so the street-level water actually has somewhere to go smart early warning systems if the lgu text_content: meet the surigao del sur meteorologist who's now with dost-pagasa blaise christian perez 24 from tandag city surigao del sur is the first graduate of a bachelor of science in meteorology in the province turning his dream into reality the surigaonon meteorologist studied at bicol university and graduated in 2025 he now works in the central office of dost-pagasa blaise shared with ato ni bai that it took him multiple routes before landing in bs meteorology bs meteorology wasn't the most conventional choice and i was very aware of that when i decided to pursue it he said he applied to several universities including adamson university and university of southeastern philippines for a different course but could not pursue it due to the pandemic he enrolled in bs medical laboratory sciences at san pedro college in davao but it didn't work for him blaise admitted that he wasn't fulfilled and struggled to stay motivated he applied again to another school but it did not work out despite these setbacks he never lost sight of his childhood dream and chose to pursue it from a young age he was fascinated by how weather worked drawing inspiration from educational channels and science books especially about natural disasters his grandmother's encouragement of his interest in science nurtured this curiosity which later guided him back to his original dream despite exploring other paths there was this persistent feeling an instinct i couldn't ignore that i should go back to what i originally wanted so i applied for bs meteorology at bicol university which had always been my first choice he recalled according to blaise meteorology was not just a chosen course it was his return to something that had always been part of him what began as a child's quiet curiosity about rain became a lifelong pursuit of understanding the atmosphere and more importantly using that understanding to serve and protect communities he said now the tandaganon meteorologist is working under the hydrometeorology division at the central office of dost-pagasa i'm working as a project technical specialist under ai4rp at dost-pagasa primarily as a researcher within the agency so far the experience has been really fulfilling he shared from what once started as curiosity i now get to work on projects that combine meteorology research and even emerging technologies like ai for disaster risk reduction beyond his research he was able to apply his expertise directly to help his community understand and respond to extreme weather events he proudly shared that he was given an opportunity to speak about the weather in the local language during coordination meetings with the tandag cdrrmo for bagyong tino and basyang these opportunities reinforced his commitment to giving back to his home province he feels a strong desire to contribute and work back in surigao del sur bringing what he has learned to help empower communities i really see the need to strengthen our local drrm efforts especially in terms of climate resilience and more importantly effective science communication sa atong early warning systems kitang tanan naka-experience kung unsa ka grabe ang epekto sa mga bagyo especially recently with ts basyang nga nagdala og grabe nga pagbaha sa atoang probinsya labi na sa tandag he said he also highlights that education and awareness are crucial and preparedness should be prioritized especially in the community people should be well-informed of pagasa forecasts including warnings and know what to do before during and after a hazard hindi man natin mapipigilan ang bagyo o ulan but through preparedness we can save lives ma minusan ang damage and make our communities more resilient he added to those planning to pursue meteorology blaise shared that they should build a strong foundation in math and physics he advised them to stay curious and explore be patient with themselves and remember that the field is not just about forecasting it is about serving people and communities padayon lang gyud even if the path feels uncertain or uncommon dili man siya popular nga course but that doesn't make it any less important if anything mas kinahanglan pa gani siya karon he shared from a curious child in tandag city to a meteorologist with plans for his home province's disaster preparedness blaise shows how passion persistence and dedication can
